I get mail in my actual (birth) name maybe about a dozen times a year. The rest of the time, I go by an alias. It took about two years to set up, and since then references to my real name have declined sharply. It really isn't that hard, nor is there any paper trail since I didn't go through the courts or petition anyone to do it legally.

One of the most "obvious" benefits to this is being able to prioritize stuff. If I get a phone call or a piece of mail addressing me by my alias, it's easier to suss out if it's bullshit. With "lower" priority accounts, I use different aliases -- I'm always surprised at which companies sell my information to whom.

We're all being tracked and watched to some extent. There's no way to ever completely disappear without significant sacrifices and outwardly bold attempts could backfire. But you can limit how much you're tracked and, if you cannot stop your information from being sold or traded, you can at least know exactly what is out there, how much and who has it. That's the next best thing and it allows me to live relatively unimpeded and without being "labeled" or standing out as unusual.

If you want something similar for yourself, you start with what is already out there. Put together a dossier on yourself, and really put time and energy into it. I recommend a physical file you can destroy when you're done. Include everything you can think of -- any time your name was used, add it. Build a timeline year by year, working backwards. Awards, arrests, diplomas, get it all together so you have a big picture.

From there, slowly "chip away" at it. Say you got a certificate of appreciation for some community service you did two years ago. Your name is on the certificate, a city website and an amateur blog as it relates to the story. You might call up the city's website, talk to some low-level pawn with access and tell them they misspelled your name. Boom, your name gets obscured. The blog is about to expire, so you either bruteforce it or buy it out for cheap and blank the whole thing.

Call old employers or colleagues and pose as someone else investigating you. See what information you're given, then work backwards -- what documents or online evidence would corroborate that story and how can you misdirect it or make it seem unreliable?

For instance, one of my aliases might be a very similar name to a man in a nearby town who is in a yacht club. Think "Smith" vs. "Smithe" or, if you can pass for it, "Gonsalez" vs. "Gonzalez." So as part of developing that particular alias, I might join a local fishing club (in a different town) using a purposefully misspelled last name. Someone who thinks they've found a place I frequent will see both myself and the unwitting decoy and think they've hit a dead end because the actual "Smithe" looks nothing like what I supposedly do. If I get fishing related junk mail to that name, I know that the club has sold my information.

All of this sounds way more complex than it is. Treat it like a hobby of sorts; junk mail companies are a great way to benchmark aliases. And whatever you do, avoid fake IDs and illegal bullshit like that. You're only obscuring yourself, and most of the time, getting your name changed gradually through "excuse me, they misspelled my name, could you change it?" works great.

Most things you sign up for ask for a lot of information, but only ever contact you by email. That's great because you can mis-enter all kinds of shit. If you're so inclined, you can bolster certain aliases with membership cards. Faking a government ID is illegal, but if I want to make a fake website for the Wildlife Preservation Society and name myself as Treasurer, a laminated membership card is like $5 and a couple hours in Photoshop. Best part of that is I can backdate it as far back as I want and control everything about that aspect of my alias.

I've given you a lot of random tidbits, but it all boils down to common sense and exactly what you want to achieve. For me, it was a "new" start and a combination of privacy and transparency of information. The government thinks I own only two firearms, my friends think I still work for a company I left five years ago, and my closest relatives have no idea what I actually do for a living, and faceberg acquaintances think I've gone back to school.
